## Prerequisites

Answer the following questions to see if you can bypass
this chapter. You can find the answers at the end of the
chapter in @sec-quiz-answers-06.

1. What is the main reason a biostatistician might move a
   long-running simulation to a cloud instance rather than
   running it on a laptop?
2. What is the difference between the AWS Management
   Console and the AWS CLI, and when would you use each?
3. How do you run an R script on a remote server without
   keeping your SSH session open?

## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- Launch an EC2 instance appropriate for a statistical
  workload (CPU, memory, storage).
- Connect to a remote server by SSH and run an R session
  there.
- Run a long job with `nohup`, `screen`, or `tmux` so it
  survives a dropped connection.
- Estimate the cost of a cloud job before launching it.
- Transfer data to and from an instance with `scp` or
  `rsync`, and to S3 for archival storage.
- Recognize when a university HPC cluster is a better fit
  than a public cloud.

## Orientation

Some analyses outgrow a laptop: multi-core simulations,
genome-scale pipelines, multi-hour model fits. The useful
question is never whether to 'move to the cloud', which is a
procurement decision rather than an analytic one, but which
specific resource you have run out of. Wall-clock time, memory,
and specialized hardware are three different shortages with
three different answers, and an analyst who has diagnosed the
shortage correctly will usually find that the cheapest adequate
remedy is not the public cloud at all.

That matters because renting a machine introduces problems a
laptop does not have. The instance bills by the hour whether or
not it is doing anything. The data have to travel, and if they
are protected health information they may not be permitted to
travel to an account you opened yourself. The job dies when the
connection does, unless you took a step nobody told you about.
This chapter covers the minimum needed to use remote compute
safely, and it argues throughout for trying an institutional
cluster before a credit card.

The dominant providers (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure)
overlap heavily; this chapter uses AWS for concreteness.
The concepts transfer. University HPC clusters serve a
similar purpose with different pricing and access
mechanisms; for many academic biostatisticians, an HPC
cluster is the first choice when one is available.

## The statistician's contribution {#sec-cloud-human}

Provisioning a machine is a form to fill in. Deciding
which machine, for how long, and with what data on it is
where the money and the compliance exposure actually
live:

**Pick the right instance.** A simulation that uses 4
cores does not benefit from a 32-core instance. A model
fit that uses 50 GB of RAM cannot run on a 16 GB
instance. Knowing the bottleneck before provisioning
prevents both under-spending (slow) and over-spending
(expensive idle cores).

**Cost discipline.** A `g4dn.12xlarge` GPU instance left
running for a weekend costs more than a small laptop.
Set budget alerts; use spot instances for fault-tolerant
work; auto-shutdown after job completion. Forgetting to
shut down is the most common cloud-cost surprise.

**Data hygiene.** Protected health data on a personal
AWS account is a compliance violation in most
institutions. Use institutional accounts; use VPC
peering to keep data inside the institutional network;
use S3 with appropriate access policies. Treat 'I'll
just upload the CSV to my personal bucket for testing'
as a red flag.

**Reproducibility off the laptop.** A cloud instance
needs the same environment specification as the laptop
that ran the analysis. Docker (@sec-docker) is the
standard answer; a `Dockerfile` plus an `renv.lock`
makes the cloud instance setup automatable.

These judgments determine whether cloud compute is a
multiplier or a money pit.

## When to use cloud compute

The decision is driven by the bottleneck, not by the
size of the dataset, and the right first question is
which resource you have run out of. @fig-compute-tier
puts the tiers in the order a working academic
biostatistician should try them.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-compute-tier
%%| fig-cap: "Choosing a compute tier. The laptop is the default and
%%|   the right place for anything interactive. A university cluster
%%|   is usually free and should be tried before a paid cloud. The
%%|   public cloud earns its cost when the cluster is unavailable,
%%|   the queue is too slow, or the job needs hardware the cluster
%%|   does not have."
flowchart TD
  A{"What have you<br/>run out of?"}
  A -->|"nothing, it is<br/>interactive work"| L["Laptop<br/><i>always the default</i>"]
  A -->|"wall-clock time,<br/>job is parallel"| Q{"University HPC<br/>available?"}
  A -->|"memory"| Q
  A -->|"specialized hardware<br/>GPU, very large RAM"| C["Public cloud<br/><i>spot for fault-tolerant work</i>"]
  Q -->|"yes"| H["SLURM plus Apptainer<br/><i>free, queued, no Docker</i>"]
  Q -->|"no, or queue<br/>too slow"| C
```

The three cases where remote compute helps are three
different shortages, and it repays being precise about
which one you have, because they are relieved by
different machines.

The first is **compute-bound, parallelizable** work: a
simulation with ten thousand independent replicates, a
bootstrap, a permutation test. The shortage is
wall-clock time and the remedy is cores. Be careful with
the arithmetic here, because the naive version of it
oversells the result: doubling the cores does not halve
the time, since the serial portion of the job does not
speed up at all and the coordination overhead grows with
the core count. The gain is nonetheless real, and for a
one-off job the cost is usually trivial against the
hours it returns.

The second is **memory-bound** work, and it differs from
the first in kind rather than in degree. A genome-scale
analysis that needs 128 GB on a laptop with 16 does not
run slowly. It does not run. Cloud instances reach into
the terabytes, and the wall-clock time on one of them
may be no better than the laptop would have managed had
the laptop been able to manage it at all. What you are
buying is feasibility, not speed, and the distinction
matters when you are justifying the cost.

The third is **long-running but robust** work: a
twenty-four-hour MCMC, a fit that must not be
interrupted. The shortage is neither cores nor memory
but the availability of your own machine, which you
would like to close, carry home, and use for something
else.

Set against these are three cases where remote compute
is the wrong answer, and they share a single cause: the
cost of a round trip to a machine that is not in front
of you. **Interactive exploration** over SSH is laggy
and unpleasant, and exploration is precisely the phase
in which you issue many small commands and look at each
result before deciding the next one. Anything
**latency-sensitive**, a Shiny app under active
debugging above all, is worse for the same reason. And a
**short analysis** is not worth provisioning at any
speed, because thirty seconds of computation is dwarfed
by the several minutes of setup, transfer, and teardown
wrapped around it.

## AWS in two pages

The Amazon Web Services landscape is vast; the subset
you need for biostatistics is small.

**EC2** (Elastic Compute Cloud): the virtual machines.
Pick an instance type (`t3.large`, `c6i.4xlarge`, etc.)
and pay per hour.

**IAM** (Identity and Access Management): users, roles,
and permissions. Create a user for yourself, generate
access keys, configure them in the AWS CLI.

**S3** (Simple Storage Service): object storage. Cheaper
than EBS for archival data; transfer to/from EC2 by
`aws s3 cp` or `rsync` over SSH.

**EBS** (Elastic Block Store): block storage for EC2.
The instance's root volume is EBS; data persists when
the instance is stopped, is gone when the instance is
terminated.

**Security Groups**: virtual firewalls. Set rules to
allow SSH (port 22) from your IP only.

**Key pairs**: SSH key pairs managed by AWS. Generate
one when you launch your first instance.

The AWS Management Console (browser GUI) is good for
learning the platform and for one-off operations. The
AWS CLI (`aws ec2 run-instances ...`) is essential for
automation and scripting.

```bash
# install
brew install awscli                  # macOS
pip install awscli                   # cross-platform

# configure once
aws configure                        # prompts for key, secret, region

# list instances
aws ec2 describe-instances --query \
  'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,InstanceType,State.Name]' \
  --output table
```

## Launching an EC2 instance

Via the Console: EC2 → Launch Instance → choose AMI
(Ubuntu LTS is a good default), choose type
(`t3.large` is a reasonable starting point at 2 vCPU,
8 GB RAM), choose a key pair, configure security
group (SSH from your IP), launch.

Via the CLI:

```bash
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0c7217cdde317cfec \
  --instance-type t3.large \
  --key-name my-keypair \
  --security-group-ids sg-0abcd1234 \
  --subnet-id subnet-0abcd1234 \
  --tag-specifications \
    'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Project,Value=readmissions}]'
```

Connect:

```bash
ssh -i ~/.ssh/my-keypair.pem ubuntu@<public-ip>
```

Once on the instance:

```bash
# install R
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y r-base r-base-dev git

# clone your project
git clone https://github.com/you/project.git
cd project
Rscript -e 'install.packages("renv"); renv::restore()'
```

Or, more reproducibly, run a Docker container with the
environment baked in (@sec-docker):

```bash
docker run -v $(pwd):/work my-analysis-image:v1.0 \
  Rscript /work/scripts/main.R
```

## Long-running jobs

You SSH in, start a job, and your laptop goes to sleep
or the hotel WiFi drops. The job dies with your shell,
and whatever it had computed dies with it.

The mechanism is worth knowing, because it explains why
each of the three remedies works and why they are not
interchangeable. When the connection closes, the shell
receives a hangup signal, `SIGHUP`, and relays it to the
processes it started; the default response to `SIGHUP`
is to terminate. Each solution below either stops the
process from receiving that signal or arranges for its
parent to be something other than the shell you are
about to lose.

**`nohup`** (no hangup): runs the command immune to
hangup signals.

```bash
nohup Rscript analysis.R > analysis.log 2>&1 &
disown                               # detach from shell
```

The process continues; output goes to `analysis.log`;
you can reconnect later and check progress with
`tail -f analysis.log`.

**`tmux`** (or `screen`, the older equivalent): a
terminal multiplexer. Start a tmux session, run the job
inside; when you disconnect, the tmux session keeps
running; reconnect with `tmux attach`.

```bash
ssh user@server
tmux new -s analysis
# inside tmux:
Rscript analysis.R
# detach with Ctrl-b d
# logout safely; come back later with:
ssh user@server
tmux attach -t analysis
```

`tmux` is also useful interactively: split panes, named
windows, persistent sessions.

**`systemd` services** for production deployments: more
involved, but appropriate when the analysis is something
that should run on a schedule.

For most ad-hoc biostatistical work, `nohup` or `tmux` is
sufficient.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: detached jobs

**Question.** You SSH into an EC2 instance, start a long
analysis with `Rscript analysis.R`, and close your
laptop. What happens to the analysis?

**Answer.**

When the SSH connection drops (or your shell exits),
the analysis process receives a hangup (SIGHUP) signal
and terminates. The job is dead; the partial output is
gone. Three remedies: (1) `nohup Rscript analysis.R &`
keeps the process running and writes its output to a
file; (2) `tmux` and `screen` provide persistent
sessions you can detach from and reattach to;
(3) systemd services run as background daemons. The
common solution for ad-hoc biostatistical work is
`tmux`. Forgetting this is the classic 'I let it run
overnight and it died' surprise.

:::

## Data transfer

To copy a file to the instance:

```bash
scp -i ~/.ssh/my-keypair.pem data.csv ubuntu@<ip>:/home/ubuntu/data/
```

For directories or incremental sync:

```bash
rsync -avz -e "ssh -i ~/.ssh/my-keypair.pem" \
  ./data/ ubuntu@<ip>:/home/ubuntu/data/
```

`rsync` only transfers changed files; useful when
iterating.

For larger or longer-term storage, S3:

```bash
# from instance to S3
aws s3 cp results.rds s3://my-bucket/project/results.rds

# from S3 to laptop
aws s3 cp s3://my-bucket/project/results.rds .

# sync directories
aws s3 sync ./output s3://my-bucket/project/output/
```

S3 is much cheaper than EBS for cold data ($0.023/GB/month
vs. $0.10 for general-purpose EBS). For data the analysis
finishes with, archive to S3.

Egress (data leaving AWS) is charged; ingress is free.
Plan large transfers accordingly.

## Cost control

Cloud billing surprises share a structure. The meter
runs on elapsed time rather than on work done, so an
idle instance costs exactly what a busy one costs, and
nothing in the system produces an event when your
analysis finishes. A laptop that has completed its job
sits there quietly; a rented machine that has completed
its job sits there quietly and bills you for the
privilege, over a weekend, in a browser tab you closed
on Friday. Every habit below is a way of supplying the
stopping event that the platform does not.

**Set budget alerts.** AWS Budgets → set a monthly
threshold; get an email when spend exceeds it.
Catches forgotten instances quickly.

**Use spot instances** for fault-tolerant work. Spot
instances are excess capacity sold at a steep discount
(60--80% off on-demand prices); the catch is that AWS
can reclaim them with two minutes' notice. For
embarrassingly-parallel simulations with checkpointing,
spot is essentially free money.

```bash
aws ec2 run-instances --instance-type c6i.xlarge \
  --instance-market-options 'MarketType=spot' \
  ...
```

**Auto-shutdown.** End your job script with `sudo shutdown -h now`
on the instance, and configure the instance to stop
(not terminate) on shutdown. The instance stops billing
once stopped (you still pay for EBS, much cheaper).

For a typical job:

```bash
# wrapper script
#!/usr/bin/env bash
Rscript analysis.R
aws s3 cp results/ s3://my-bucket/project/results/ --recursive
sudo shutdown -h now
```

The instance does the analysis, uploads results, shuts
down. You wake up to results in S3 and a stopped
instance.

## Alternatives to AWS

**Google Cloud Platform** (GCP). Comparable to AWS;
slightly different terminology. Strong for ML-heavy
workloads via Vertex AI.

**Azure**. Microsoft's cloud. Strong if your
institution is in the Microsoft ecosystem (Office 365
single-sign-on, Active Directory).

**DigitalOcean**, **Linode**. Simpler, cheaper for
small-scale work. Less to learn; fewer features.

**University HPC clusters**. SLURM-based job
submission, often free for affiliated researchers,
typically have R, Python, and standard scientific
libraries pre-installed. The right first stop for
academic work when available; the queue waits and
shared environment are the trade-offs.

One trade-off deserves more than a mention, because it
collides with @sec-docker. Most HPC clusters do not permit
Docker, and for a good reason: the Docker daemon runs as
root, and a shared multi-tenant cluster cannot grant every
user root. The standard substitute is **Apptainer**
(formerly Singularity), a container runtime designed for
exactly this setting, which runs unprivileged and can build
its image directly from your Docker image
[@kurtzer2017singularity]:

```bash
# on the cluster, convert the image you already built
apptainer pull analysis.sif docker://ghcr.io/you/analysis:v1.0

# run the pipeline inside it, under SLURM
srun apptainer exec analysis.sif Rscript scripts/main.R
```

The reproducibility argument of @sec-docker survives the
move intact: the image is the same image, and the pinned
environment is the same environment. Only the runtime
changes. Discovering this at the point of submitting your
first cluster job, rather than in advance, is a common and
avoidable afternoon.

Within a single node, the parallelism is R's own. The
`future` framework [@bengtsson2021future] lets the same
code run sequentially on your laptop and across the
cluster's cores by changing one line, the plan, which keeps
the parallel and serial versions of an analysis from
diverging.

For most academic biostatistics work, the priority
ordering is: laptop (interactive), university HPC
(batch), AWS/GCP (when HPC is unavailable or
inadequate).

## Worked example: a simulation on AWS

```bash
# 1. provision
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0c7217cdde317cfec \
  --instance-type c6i.4xlarge \
  --key-name my-keypair \
  --security-group-ids sg-0abcd1234 \
  --subnet-id subnet-0abcd1234 \
  --instance-initiated-shutdown-behavior stop \
  --user-data file://bootstrap.sh \
  --tag-specifications \
    'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Project,Value=sim2026}]'

# bootstrap.sh installs R, clones the repo, runs the simulation,
# uploads results to S3, and shuts down

# 2. wait for it to finish (and shut down)
aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids <id> \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].State.Name'

# 3. retrieve results
aws s3 cp s3://my-bucket/sim2026/results.rds .

# 4. terminate the instance (delete it for good)
aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids <id>
```

The cost: a 4-hour run on `c6i.4xlarge` (16 vCPU, 32 GB)
at $0.68/hour is about $2.72. EBS storage another
$0.50. S3 egress for the results, pennies.

For a simulation that took 32 hours on a laptop, this is
a 8× speedup at $3 in costs. The judgment is whether
the time saved is worth $3.

## Collaborating with an LLM on cloud setup

LLMs handle AWS recipes well; they sometimes generate
shell scripts with subtle cost or security issues.

**Prompt 1: choosing an instance.** Describe the
workload (cores, memory, expected runtime, parallel
nature) and ask: 'recommend an EC2 instance type and
estimate the cost.'

*What to watch for.* Verify against the current AWS
pricing page (LLMs may quote out-of-date prices).
Double-check the instance type matches the workload
type (compute-optimized vs. memory-optimized).

*Verification.* The AWS pricing calculator is the
ground truth.

**Prompt 2: scripting a cloud job.** Describe the job
and ask the LLM to write a shell script that
provisions, runs, and cleans up.

*What to watch for.* Failure handling: what if the
script crashes partway? Does the instance still shut
down? Does the data still upload to S3? LLM scripts
often miss these.

*Verification.* Run the script with a deliberate failure
inserted; verify cleanup still happens.

**Prompt 3: diagnosing AWS errors.** Paste the error
message and ask the LLM to diagnose.

*What to watch for.* Common errors (security group not
allowing SSH, instance not yet running, key pair
mismatch) are easy. Less common errors (IAM role
issues, VPC peering) get mixed answers; verify against
AWS documentation.

*Verification.* The AWS console is the source of truth
for instance state; check it before assuming the LLM is
right.

## Principle in use

Three habits keep the bill and the science both under control:

1. **Provision deliberately, shut down promptly.** The
   instance is billed every hour it runs, including
   while you sleep.
2. **Script it.** A shell script that provisions, runs,
   and cleans up is the only way to make a cloud job
   reproducible.
3. **Use the right tier.** University HPC for free
   academic compute; AWS/GCP when scale demands; spot
   instances for fault-tolerant parallel work; on-demand
   only when you must.

## Exercises

1. Launch a `t3.medium` EC2 instance in the AWS free
   tier (or equivalent). Install R, clone a GitHub
   repository, and run a simple analysis. Shut the
   instance down when finished. Document every cost.
2. Run a 1-hour simulation on an EC2 instance using
   `nohup`. Disconnect your laptop and reconnect; verify
   the simulation is still running.
3. Set up an S3 bucket and transfer a dataset to and
   from your EC2 instance. Compute the data-transfer
   charge.
4. Compare the cost of running a 4-hour simulation on
   AWS spot vs. on-demand vs. on a university HPC.
   Document each.
5. Write a wrapper script that provisions, runs, and
   shuts down an EC2 instance for a single R script.
   Test that it cleans up even when the script fails.

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-06}

1. Cloud compute provides more resources (CPU, RAM,
   storage) than a laptop, on demand, without capital
   investment. A 10-hour simulation on a laptop can be
   a 1-hour simulation on an 8-core cloud instance, and
   the laptop stays free for other work. Cloud compute
   also keeps research data off personal machines and
   provides audit logs. The trade-off is cost, security
   complexity, and data-transfer overhead.
2. The AWS Management Console is a browser-based GUI;
   good for one-off instance launches, inspecting
   state, and learning the platform. The AWS CLI is a
   command-line tool; essential for automation,
   scripting, and reproducible infrastructure setup.
   Most professional workflows use the CLI for routine
   work and the Console for debugging. The CLI also
   composes naturally with shell scripts and `make`.
3. Use `nohup Rscript analysis.R > analysis.log 2>&1 &`
   to detach the process from the shell, or launch
   inside a `tmux` or `screen` session that persists
   after logout. The process continues running; its
   output goes to the log file; you reconnect later
   with `tail -f analysis.log` or `tmux attach`.
   Without one of these, closing your shell kills the
   job.
